title: Understanding Your Blood Test Results: A Complete Guide
summary: Learn how to interpret common blood markers like CBC, cholesterol, glucose, and liver function tests.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
Blood tests are one of the most common diagnostic tools used by healthcare providers. Understanding what those numbers mean can help you take charge of your health.

Complete Blood Count (CBC)

The CBC measures red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Abnormal values can indicate anemia, infection, or blood disorders.

Metabolic Panel

Tests like glucose, creatinine, and electrolytes provide insights into kidney function, diabetes risk, and hydration status.

When to Consult Your Doctor

Always discuss results with your healthcare provider. Lab values should be interpreted in context of your symptoms and medical history.

title: What is Hemoglobin A1C and Why It Matters
summary: Discover why HbA1c is the gold standard for monitoring diabetes and blood sugar control over time.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
Hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) is a critical marker that reflects your average blood sugar levels over the past 2-3 months.

Target Ranges

For most adults with diabetes, the target is below 7%. Non-diabetic individuals typically have values below 5.7%.

Why Three Months?

Red blood cells live approximately 120 days. As glucose circulates in your blood, it binds to hemoglobin, creating a 'glycated' form that serves as a long-term record.

Regular monitoring helps prevent complications like neuropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular disease.

title: Thyroid Function Tests: TSH, T3, and T4 Explained
summary: A comprehensive guide to understanding thyroid lab tests and what they reveal about your metabolism.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
Thyroid hormones regulate metabolism, energy, and mood. Testing typically includes TSH, free T4, and sometimes T3.

TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone)

Produced by the pituitary gland, TSH tells your thyroid to make more hormones. High TSH suggests hypothyroidism; low TSH suggests hyperthyroidism.

Free T4 and T3

These are the actual thyroid hormones. T4 is the storage form, while T3 is the active form used by cells.

Common Conditions

Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease are common autoimmune thyroid disorders that show up in these tests.

title: Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know
summary: Understanding HDL, LDL, and triglycerides to protect your heart health.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
Cholesterol is essential for cell function, but too much of the wrong type increases heart disease risk.

LDL: The 'Bad' Cholesterol

Low-density lipoprotein carries cholesterol to arteries where it can build up as plaque. Target: below 100 mg/dL for most people.

HDL: The 'Good' Cholesterol

High-density lipoprotein removes cholesterol from arteries. Higher is better: aim for above 60 mg/dL.

Triglycerides

High triglycerides often indicate metabolic syndrome or increased cardiovascular risk. Target: below 150 mg/dL.

title: Kidney Function Tests: Creatinine and BUN
summary: How creatinine, BUN, and eGFR tests assess kidney health and detect early disease.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
Kidneys filter waste from your blood. Lab tests measure how well they're working.

Creatinine

A waste product from muscle metabolism. Elevated levels suggest reduced kidney function.

BUN (Blood Urea Nitrogen)

Measures nitrogen from protein breakdown. High BUN can indicate kidney problems or dehydration.

eGFR (Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate)

Calculated from creatinine, age, and sex. Values below 60 may indicate chronic kidney disease.

title: Liver Enzymes: ALT and AST Explained
summary: What elevated liver enzymes mean and when to be concerned about liver health.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
ALT and AST are enzymes released when liver cells are damaged.

ALT (Alanine Aminotransferase)

More specific to liver damage. Elevated in hepatitis, fatty liver disease, and medication toxicity.

AST (Aspartate Aminotransferase)

Found in liver, heart, and muscles. Less specific than ALT but useful in combination.

When to Worry

Mild elevations are common and often temporary. Persistent elevation or values more than 2-3x normal require investigation.

title: Vitamin D Deficiency: Testing and Treatment
summary: Why vitamin D matters for bone health, immunity, and mood—and how to test your levels.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
Vitamin D deficiency is widespread, affecting over 40% of adults in some regions.

Testing: 25-Hydroxy Vitamin D

This is the standard test. Optimal levels are 30-50 ng/mL. Below 20 is deficient.

Why It Matters

Vitamin D supports calcium absorption, immune function, and mood regulation. Deficiency increases risk of osteoporosis and fractures.

Supplementation

Most people need 1000-2000 IU daily. Some require higher doses based on test results.

title: Inflammation Markers: CRP and ESR
summary: How C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate detect inflammation in your body.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
Inflammation markers help diagnose infections, autoimmune diseases, and chronic conditions.

CRP (C-Reactive Protein)

Rises rapidly in response to inflammation. High-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) predicts cardiovascular risk.

ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate)

Measures how quickly red blood cells settle. Elevated in infections, autoimmune diseases, and some cancers.

Clinical Use

These tests are nonspecific but useful for monitoring disease activity in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis.

title: Electrolyte Imbalances: Sodium, Potassium, and More
summary: Understanding electrolyte levels and their role in nerve function, hydration, and heart rhythm.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
Electrolytes are minerals that carry electrical charges and are essential for cellular function.

Sodium

Regulates fluid balance. Low sodium (hyponatremia) causes confusion and weakness.

Potassium

Critical for heart rhythm. Both high and low levels can be life-threatening.

Calcium and Magnesium

Important for bone health, muscle contraction, and enzyme function.

title: Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) Test: What Men Should Know
summary: PSA screening for prostate health: benefits, limitations, and what elevated levels mean.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
PSA is a protein produced by the prostate. Elevated levels may indicate prostate cancer, but can also result from benign conditions.

Normal Ranges

PSA below 4 ng/mL is typically normal, but age and prostate size matter. Trends over time are more important than single values.

False Positives

Prostatitis (infection) and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) can elevate PSA without cancer being present.

Screening Debate

Guidelines vary. Discuss with your doctor whether screening is right for you based on age, family history, and risk factors.

title: Complete Metabolic Panel (CMP) Explained
summary: A detailed look at the 14 tests included in a CMP and what they reveal about your health.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
The CMP is a comprehensive screening tool that assesses kidney function, liver function, electrolytes, and blood sugar.

What's Included

Glucose, calcium, sodium, potassium, CO2, chloride, BUN, creatinine, albumin, total protein, ALP, ALT, AST, and bilirubin.

Why Doctors Order It

It's a cost-effective way to screen for multiple conditions and monitor chronic diseases like diabetes and kidney disease.

title: Iron Studies and Anemia Testing
summary: Understanding ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, and transferrin saturation in diagnosing iron deficiency.
author: Lab Lens Team
content:
Iron is essential for red blood cell production. Deficiency causes fatigue and anemia.

Ferritin

Reflects total body iron stores. Low ferritin indicates iron deficiency; very high levels suggest inflammation or hemochromatosis.

Serum Iron and TIBC

Serum iron measures circulating iron. TIBC (total iron-binding capacity) shows how much transferrin is available to carry iron.

Treatment

Iron supplements or dietary changes (red meat, spinach, fortified cereals) can correct deficiency.
